Step 1, interest. Put $100 in the bank at 5 % a year, and after one year you have $105.

Why quants care: discounting is everywhere in quantitative finance. In theory, the price of an investment is the money it is expected to pay you, discounted back to today.

caption:
➡️ Quant Finance from scratch part 5: Measuring returns

Two questions guide the video: why does a fall hurt more than the same rise helps, and how do quants measure returns so that they add up?

Step 1, the base. A return is always measured from where you start. From $100, minus 50 % takes away $50. From $50, plus 50 % adds back only $25, so you are still $25 short.

Step 2, percent moves multiply. $100 × ½ = $50, and only × 2 brings you back to $100. Times 2 is +100 %.

Step 3, percent returns don't add up. −50 % + 100 % makes +50 % on paper, yet the money is right back at $100.

Step 4, the log return: the natural log of the new price divided by the old one. The fall becomes ln(0.5) = −0.69, the rise ln(2) = +0.69, and together they make exactly 0.

Step 5, the idea behind it. On a log scale every halving is the same step down and every doubling the same step up. The log return is the length of that step, so a fall and the rise that undoes it have the same size.

Step 6, a whole year. A simulated stock moves randomly, about 2 % a day. Adding up its 252 daily percent moves gives −24.0 %, yet it really lost 25.0 %. Adding up the daily log returns and turning the sum back into percent gives exactly the real −25.0 %.

Why quants love log returns: they add up over time, a price built from them can never fall below zero, and in the classic model of a stock the log returns follow the bell curve from part 4.

The honest part: for one small day both are almost the same, since +1 % is 0.00995 as a log return. The difference grows with big moves and over time.

caption:
➡️ Quant Finance from scratch Part 8: the Sharpe ratio, in 16 lines of Python you can follow line by line.

Two simulated investments: the wild one is built to earn 12 % a year with a volatility of 24 %, the calm one 6 % a year with a volatility of 3 %.

Step 1, subtract the safe rate. A safe account pays interest without any risk, here 3 % a year. Only the return above it is the reward for taking risk.

Step 2, divide by the risk. The extra return divided by the volatility is the Sharpe ratio: the extra return you get for every unit of risk.

Step 3, measure it. Over 10,000 simulated years, the wild one averaged 11.7 % a year with a volatility of 24.0 %, a Sharpe ratio of 0.36. The calm one averaged 6.0 % with a volatility of 3.0 %, a Sharpe ratio of 0.99.

Step 4, a fair comparison. Put one eighth of the money into the wild one and the rest into the safe account. The mix swings exactly as much as the calm one, 3.0 % a year, and earns only 4.1 %, while the calm one earns 6.0 %.

Step 5, why the ratio is fair. The mix still has a Sharpe ratio of 0.36. Mixing with cash only moves you along the same line, so the ratio measures the investment itself.

Step 6, what the wild one would need. To be as good a deal as the calm one at its own risk, it would have to earn 26.8 % a year.

So twice the return for eight times the risk is a bad deal here: per unit of risk, the calm one pays about 2.7 times as much.

Why quants care: the Sharpe ratio is one of the most used numbers for comparing investments and strategies. It is named after William F. Sharpe, who introduced it in 1966 and later shared the 1990 Nobel prize in economics. One catch: it treats swings up and down the same, and a strategy with rare big crashes can look better than it is until the crash comes.

caption:
➡️ Quant Finance from scratch Part 9: volatility drag.

Step 1, plus 50 %, then minus 50 %. Start with $100. Gain 50 % and you have $150, lose 50 % and you have $75. The average of the two returns is 0 %, yet you are down 25 %.

Step 2, why. The gain added $50, but the loss took half of $150, which is $75. Percent moves multiply (Part 5), so the loss hits a bigger pile.

Step 3, the square. Up and down by the same percent s leaves (1 + s) × (1 − s) = 1 − s² of your money: $99 for 10 %, $75 for 50 %.

Step 4, the rule. Per step that is about half the swing squared. This is volatility drag: your money grows at about the average return minus half the volatility squared.

Step 5, the test. Two simulated investments, both built for 10 % a year on average, with a volatility of 10 % and 50 %. Over 10,000 simulated years the calm one averaged 9.9 % with a growth rate of 9.4 %, while the wild one averaged 11.0 % and its money shrank by 1.5 % a year.

Step 6, the rule predicted both. Half the volatility squared is 0.5 % for calm and 12.5 % for wild: five times the swing, 25 times the drag, more than its whole average. Average minus drag gives 9.4 % and minus 1.5 %, matching the simulation to one decimal.

So is your average return lying? It leaves out the drag.

The average return is the average daily return times 252. The growth rate is the average daily log return times 252 (Part 5), the rate the money compounds at. The rule is approximate: for plus and minus 50 % the exact loss per step is 13.4 % against its 12.5 %.

Why quants care: in the classic stock price model, the typical path grows at the average minus half the variance. The same drag hits funds that reset their leverage daily.

caption:
➡️ Quant Finance from scratch part 10: correlation

Correlation is one number between −1 and 1, and it shapes how risky a portfolio is. This video shows you what it measures.

Step 1, two assets and one hidden market. Every day the simulated market gives both assets the same push, and each gets its own push, typically half as big. Each asset is built to swing 20 % a year.

Step 2, the cloud. Put each day on a map, A's move across and B's move up. Their own pushes alone would make a round cloud, and the shared market stretches it along a rising line.

Step 3, what it measures. Put every move in typical swings (distance from its average divided by its standard deviation), multiply the two moves of each day and take the average. Moving the same way counts plus, moving apart counts minus. Over 10,000 simulated years this pair scores +0.80.

Step 4, the scale. The average always lands between −1 and +1. At +1 every point sits on a rising line, at −1 on a falling line, and at 0 the cloud is round.

Step 5, cause. Correlation never tells you which one causes the other. Here neither does, because the hidden market moves both.

Step 6, risk. Put half your money in each. Each asset alone swings 20.0 % a year, and the 50/50 mix swings 19.0 % at a correlation of +0.80, 14.1 % at 0 and 10.0 % at −0.50.

The code builds every pair from the same market and the same noise, weighted with the square roots of |c| and 1 − |c|, so each asset keeps its 20 % (variances add, Part 3). The average of the products is exactly the Pearson correlation.

Why it matters: portfolio risk depends on how assets move together, the core of Harry Markowitz's "Portfolio Selection" (Journal of Finance, 1952; Nobel prize 1990). One catch: correlations measured in calm times can rise when markets fall. Longin and Solnik (Journal of Finance, 2001) found that the correlation between the largest stock markets increases in bear markets.

➡️ Part 1 of learning Quant Finance from scratch

Two questions guide the video: what exactly is an edge, and why does a tiny edge turn into near certainty?

Step 1, probability. The wheel has 37 pockets and 18 of them are red, so a bet on red wins with a probability of 18 out of 37, just under half.

Step 2, expected value. A win pays one dollar and a loss costs one dollar. Weighted by their chances, that averages out to minus 2.7 cents per bet.

Step 3, one player. A single spin pays plus or minus one dollar, so a balance jumps around. Our example player was 11 dollars ahead after 47 spins and still ended 22 dollars down.

Step 4, a thousand players. Their balances spread out like stock charts, and 181 of the 1,000 walked away with a profit.

Step 5, the casino. It takes the other side of all one million bets and earns $27,288, within one percent of the expected $27,027.

Step 6, the law of large numbers. The more bets you add up, the closer the average gets to the expected value. The casino's profit per bet settles at 2.7 cents.

Step 7, the reason. The edge grows with every bet, while luck only grows with the square root of the number of bets. After about 1,400 bets the edge is bigger than one standard deviation of luck.

The same idea runs insurance companies, market makers and quant funds: they look for a small edge and repeat it many thousands of times. Even the casino was 44 dollars down after its first 2,000 bets, which is why measuring risk matters as much as measuring the edge.

The random walk 

Two questions guide the video: what exactly is a random walk, and what does the drift do?

Step 1, the coin. Heads moves the price up one dollar, tails moves it down one dollar, and every flip is fifty fifty.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance From Scratch, Part 3: The Square Root Rule

Take a hundred random steps, left or right, and most of the time you end up within about ten steps of where you started. That is the square root rule.

Two questions guide the video: why is this rule so important in quantitative finance, and what does it mean for a stock?

Step 1, a thousand prices. Each one moves $1 up or down per step, like a coin flip, for 400 steps. A few end up far away, and most stay surprisingly close to the start.

Step 2, the spread. The standard deviation is the typical distance from the middle: about $5 after 25 steps, $10 after 100 and $20 after 400. Four times the steps give twice the spread.

Step 3, why a square root. Ups and downs cancel each other out, while their squares only add up. That sum is the variance: 100 after 100 steps (99.6 in our run), and its square root is 10. That is the ten from the start: 73 % of the prices end within $10.

Step 4, the drift from part 2. It grows in a straight line, the randomness only with the square root. From 25 to 4,000 steps the drift grew 160 times and the randomness about 13 times, so the share of prices below their start fell from 43 % to 4 %.

Step 5, a stock. Say it moves 1 % up or down a day. A year of 252 trading days gives 1 % × √252 = 15.9 %, and 66 % of 20,000 simulated years ended inside that range. With a drift of 6.8 % a year, the chance to end above the start grows from 64 % after one year to 91 % after ten, in this simple model.

Why quants care: the rule turns daily risk into yearly risk, and it sits inside every option price, because a later deadline leaves the price more room to move.

The honest part: the rule assumes independent steps, and real markets have calm and wild phases. It is a first estimate, and later parts show where it breaks. Everything is simulated with a fixed seed, nothing was downloaded, and every number comes from a real run of the code.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance From Scratch, Part 4: The Bell Curve

This is the bell curve, the most important curve in quantitative finance theory, and this video shows you why.

Two questions guide the video: why do random steps always build this same shape, and what does it let quants say about how far a stock can move?

Step 1, the board. 1,000 balls fall through 12 rows of pins and bounce right or left like a coin flip. Every ball is a random walk from part 2, and the bin where it lands counts how often it went right.

Step 2, why the middle. All 4,096 paths are equally likely. Only one goes right every time, while 924 go right exactly six times and end in the middle, so most balls land there: 613 of 1,000 in the middle three bins.

Step 3, part 3 again. The 1,000 walks from part 3 build the same bell after 400 steps, only wider: their spread is 19.9, the square root rule's √400 = 20.

Step 4, any step shape. Add up a hundred random amounts, each anywhere between -1 and +1, and the bell appears again. That is the central limit theorem.

Step 5, the rule. The bell is the normal distribution: about 68 % of results land within one standard deviation, 95 % within two and 99.7 % within three. Our 100,000 sums gave 68.2, 95.5 and 99.7 %.

Step 6, a stock. A year is the sum of many daily moves, so quants model returns with the bell. With 1 % a day the yearly swing is 1 % × √252 = 15.9 %: about two years in three end within 16 % up or down, nineteen in twenty within 32 %, and the bell says a move beyond 48 % comes once in about 370 years.

caption:
➡️ Part 31 of Quantitative Finance From Scratch: implied volatility. 

The Black-Scholes formula from part 30 needs five inputs. Four of them you can look up (stock price, strike, rate and time), but the fifth, the volatility over the life of the option, lies in the future. Traders form their own views, buy and sell options, and supply and demand set the price. Put that market price into the formula and solve it backwards for the volatility, and you get the implied volatility.

Our test run (impliedvol.py, 16 lines of plain Python): stock 100, strike 100, rate 5 %, 1 year, and a call that costs 12 dollars on the market. The volatility sits in several places of the formula, so there is no way to solve for it by hand, but the price always rises with the volatility. A bisection search tries the middle of the range (50 %, 25 %, 12.5 % and so on) and halves the range each time. After 10 steps the price fits to half a cent, and the implied volatility is 24.1 %.

Every strike and every expiry date has its own implied volatility. Together all these values form the implied volatility surface. Historical volatility, measured from past returns, serves as a comparison, and as the estimate when no options trade.

caption:
➡️ Part 32 of Quantitative Finance From Scratch: put call parity. 

A call gives you the right to buy a stock at the strike on a fixed date, and a put gives you the right to sell it at that price. If you buy a call and sell a put with the same strike and the same date, you end up buying the stock at the strike whatever happens, because above the strike you use your call, and below it the buyer of your put sells you the stock. That sure deal is worth the stock price today minus the present value of the strike, so the call minus the put equals the stock minus the present value of the strike.

Our test run (putcall.py, 16 lines of plain Python) prices both options with Black Scholes for a stock and a strike of 100 dollars, a rate of 5 %, one year and a volatility of 20 %. The call costs 10.45 dollars and the put 5.57 dollars, and their difference of 4.88 dollars equals 100 minus 95.12, the present value of the strike. Six end prices drawn with seed 32 show that the call minus the put always pays the end price minus the strike.

The rule needs no model for the stock price (Merton 1973), so traders use it to check quotes and to turn a call price into a put price. It holds exactly for European options, which can only be used at expiry, on stocks without dividends.

American options and dividends change it.

Delta is how much the price of an option moves when the stock moves by one dollar. Step 1, three simulated assets with assumed numbers, not forecasts: A, like bonds, earns 4 % a year at 6 % risk (volatility), B, like stocks, 7 % at 18 %, and C, like a riskier stock, 11 % at 25 %. Step 4, many betas: a factor model gives a stock one beta per factor. There is a lot of discussion in science ongoing whether it is still a good estimate for expected returns or too simple with just 1 factor (market). Still its crucial to understand the concept itsself.

Our game is simulated: a coin that wins 55% of the time, and every bet pays even money. 1,000 players start with $100 each and bet the same share of their money on each of 1,000 flips. Every bet size gets exactly the same flips, so only the size changes.

➡️ Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 19: value at risk (VaR).

Value at risk is the maximum loss that a portfolio should not exceed over a chosen period, with a chosen probability called the confidence level, under normal market conditions. A VaR of 2% over one day at 99% means: on 99 days out of 100, the loss of a single day stays below 2%.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance From Scratch, Part 20: Backtesting.

A backtest tests a trading strategy on historical data, as if you had used it back then, to see whether it would have made money and how much risk it took along the way. Portfolio managers, analysts and quant researchers run backtests before real money goes into an idea.

The key idea: split the past in two. You build the rule on the first part (in sample) and then test it on later data it has never seen (out of sample). The out of sample result is the fairer check.

Why it matters: if you search the past hard enough, you will find patterns, even in pure noise. Trying rule after rule until one looks good is called data mining, and many of those patterns are just statistical chance.

In this video we test 498 simple rules (hold after the price rose or fell over 2 to 250 days) on 10 simulated years of a market with no edge at all. The best rule in the first five years makes +11% in sample. On the next five years, data it has never seen, the same rule loses 28% and drops to rank 460 of 498. The ten best rules in sample lose 18.5% on average out of sample.

Even a properly backtested result only describes the past. Markets change, and a pattern that worked for years can stop working.

Classic mistakes: look-ahead bias (using information you could not have known at that time), survivorship bias (testing only companies that still exist today) and leaving out trading costs.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance From Scratch, Part 21: Linear Regression in finance 

Linear regression finds the straight line that best describes how one quantity moves with another. In finance, that is often a stock's daily return against the market's daily return.

Least squares: for every day, you measure how far the real return lies from the line, square that distance and add everything up. The best line makes this sum as small as possible.

The line has two numbers. The slope is the beta from Part 14: how strongly the stock follows the market. The intercept is alpha: what the stock earns on average on a day when the market does not move. What the line cannot explain is the residual, and R² tells you which share of the swings (the variance) the line explains, from 0 for nothing to 1 for everything.

In this video we simulate two years (504 trading days) of a market and a stock with a built-in beta of 1.2, a second factor with a beta of 0.6 and no alpha. The line finds a beta of 1.26 (the 1.2 lies within the range of chance for two years of data), an alpha of +0.05% a day and an R² of 52%. With two inputs, the line becomes a plane: betas 1.27 and 0.60, R² 63%.

Quants use regression to estimate betas, to size hedges, to test whether a strategy earns more than its risk, and to check whether two assets really move together.

The limits: a regression only finds a relationship in the data you give it. It does not prove that one thing causes the other, a few extreme days can pull the line (three invented extreme days move our slope from 1.26 to 1.10), and a relationship from the past can change.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance From Scratch, Part 22: Hypothesis Testing.

You start with the null hypothesis: the strategy's true average return is zero, so there is no edge. Then you ask how often pure luck would produce a result at least as extreme as yours if that were true.

The t statistic divides the average return by its standard error (the typical size of the random error in an average). The p value is the probability of a t statistic at least this far from zero when there is really no edge. At the 95% confidence level, a result counts as significant when the p value is below 5%, and that matches a 95% confidence interval that does not include zero.

In this video we simulate a strategy with a small real edge built in (a true Sharpe ratio of 1, daily swings of 1%) for five years. It reaches a t statistic of 1.50 and a two-sided p value of 13.3%. The 95% interval for the average daily return goes from -0.013% to +0.096%, so it includes zero and the result is not significant at the 5% level, even though the edge is real. By chance, the run only showed a Sharpe ratio of 0.67 instead of 1, and five years of data were not enough this time.

A useful rule: the t statistic is about the yearly Sharpe ratio times the square root of the number of years. With a Sharpe ratio of 1, you need about four years to reach a t statistic of 2.

The biggest trap is testing many rules. Test 100 strategies with no edge at all, and about 5 will still pass at the 5% level by luck. In our run, 7 did.

A p value is not the probability that your strategy works. The test assumes independent returns and a market that stays the same, and a real edge can still be too small to survive trading costs.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance From Scratch, Part 23: Mean Reversion.

Mean reversion means that a quantity which moves far from its long run average tends to drift back toward it. A single stock price behaves much like a random walk, but spreads, ratios and rates (the gap between two related stocks, interest rates, volatility) often show a pull back.

The simplest model: every day the distance from the average shrinks by a fixed share, plus a random shock. The half life is the time it takes for half of that distance to disappear, so a short half life means a strong pull back.

To test for the pull, you regress today's change on yesterday's distance from the average. A negative slope means a pull back. But even pure chance often looks like a pull here: in our test, 34% of pure random walks passed the usual limit of -2. So quants use a stricter limit for the t statistic of about -3 (the Dickey-Fuller limit, about -2.9).

In this video we simulate one spread with a built-in half life of 10 days for four years. The regression finds a slope of -0.070, a t statistic of -6.05 and a half life of 9.5 days, far beyond that limit. The z score measures how many standard deviations the spread is from its average.

Is it profitable? Only if the pull is real, strong enough to beat trading costs and still there in data you did not use for testing. A 2016 study of 97 published return signals found that their returns were on average 58% lower after publication. The average can shift, the pull can vanish, and a spread can keep widening before it comes back. caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance From Scratch, Part 24: Momentum.

Momentum means that assets which rose the most over the past months tend to keep rising a little longer, and the biggest losers tend to keep falling. It is the opposite of mean reversion from part 23. Quants usually measure it as the return over the past 12 months, leaving out the most recent month, because very short moves tend to reverse.

In research, a classic momentum portfolio ranks many stocks by this past return, buys the top group, sells the bottom group and repeats this every month. In practice there are two common versions: long only (you only hold the top ranked stocks, for example through a momentum fund) and long short (winners minus losers, so the ups and downs of the whole market largely cancel out).

In this video we simulate 500 stocks for 30 years with a small built-in continuation: expected returns that drift slowly. The long short version earns 5.9% a year with a t statistic of 6.00 and a beta of -0.01 to the market. The long only version earns 13.7% a year, but with a beta of 0.99 it moves almost one for one with the market, which itself earned 10.5% a year in this simulated path.

Momentum has been found in stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, and in more than 200 years of stock data. It also has a dangerous side: after a market fall, a sharp rebound can lift the past losers fast, and momentum portfolios have had sudden, very large losses, for example in spring 2009. Some studies find it weaker and more volatile in recent decades, and trading costs eat a part of it, but it has not disappeared.

caption:
➡️Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 35: how market makers make money. 

The first source is the spread. Like an exchange booth, a market maker buys a little below the fair price at the bid and sells a little above it at the ask, so every trade earns half the gap whatever the stock does next. After selling a call, it buys delta shares, so small moves no longer matter. The second source comes from the other Greeks: theta is the income, because the call it owes loses value every day, and gamma is the cost, because after every big move it must buy shares high and sell them low to keep the hedge. If the stock moves exactly as much as the implied volatility in the price, income and cost cancel. If it stays calmer, the market maker earns, and if it moves more, it loses. caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 36: how the order book works. 

The order book is the list of all waiting orders for one stock: buyers on one side with the prices they will pay, sellers on the other with the prices they want. These waiting orders are limit orders, buy or sell, but only at this price or better. The highest bid and the lowest ask are the best prices, and the gap between them is the spread. A market order does not wait and trades right away against the best orders on the other side. If it is larger than what waits at the best price, it eats through the next levels, every level costs a little more (slippage), and a large buy order pushes the price up. Market makers keep limit orders on both sides, buy at the bid and sell at the ask, and the spread is what they earn. Depth decides how much a large order moves the price.

The code (orderbook.py, 16 lines) simulates 30,000 random limit orders, market orders and cancellations with price time priority. The average spread was 3.19 cents, and one market buy for 20,000 shares moved the best ask from $97.63 to $97.71, 8 cents, at an average price 4.10 cents above the old best ask.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 39: GARCH. 

Markets show a clear pattern: calm weeks follow calm weeks, and high volatility days arrive in groups. This is called volatility clustering. Robert Engle introduced the idea in 1982 with the ARCH model (Econometrica), Tim Bollerslev extended it to GARCH in 1986 (Journal of Econometrics), and Engle received the 2003 Nobel Prize in economics for methods of analyzing time series with time-varying volatility.

GARCH(1,1) builds tomorrow's variance, the square of volatility, from three parts: a small constant omega that pulls the forecast back toward a normal level, today's move squared times a weight alpha, so a big surprise raises tomorrow's forecast right away, and today's variance times a weight beta, the memory that keeps a high forecast high for a while.

The code (garch_reel.py, 16 lines of Python with numpy) uses typical values omega 0.05, alpha 0.10 and beta 0.85, in percent squared per day. The normal level is a volatility of 1 % a day. After a drop of 4 % on a calm day, tomorrow's variance is 0.05 + 0.10 x 16 + 0.85 x 1 = 2.50, so the forecast volatility jumps to 1.58 %. The extra variance then halves every 13.5 trading days: the forecast for day 5 is 1.49 %, for day 10 1.39 % and for day 30 1.16 %. In 1,000,000 simulated days of the same model, a move above 2.5 % happens on 1.75 % of all days, but on 10.97 % of the days right after such a move, about 6.3 times as often.

Risk managers use GARCH forecasts to update value at risk, and some funds scale their positions down when the forecast volatility rises. If you want the full picture, there is a longer GARCH video on the YouTube channel.

caption:
➡️Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 40: GJR GARCH. 

The goal is simple: forecast how big tomorrow's moves will be. Volatility comes in clusters, and plain GARCH uses that by building tomorrow's forecast from today's move squared and today's forecast. Squaring wipes out the sign, though, so a 4 % drop and a 4 % rise raise tomorrow's forecast by exactly the same amount.

In real stock markets a drop raises volatility much more than a rise of the same size. One reason is leverage: when the price falls, the company's debt weighs more relative to its stock, so the stock itself becomes riskier. Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle captured this in 1993 with one extra weight, gamma, that only switches on after a down day. The model is now known as GJR GARCH: tomorrow's variance = omega + (alpha + gamma x I) x today's move squared + beta x today's variance, where I is 1 after a down day and 0 otherwise.

The code (gjr_reel.py, 16 lines of Python with numpy) uses typical values omega 0.02, alpha 0.02, gamma 0.12 and beta 0.90, in percent squared per day, so the normal level is a volatility of 1 % a day. caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 41: Volatility Targeting. 

In quant finance, risk is usually measured as volatility, how strongly a price swings up and down. Volatility comes in clusters, so stormy days tend to follow stormy days, and that makes it possible to forecast it to some extent. GARCH from parts 39 and 40 is one way to do that; rolling averages and exponentially weighted averages are others.

Volatility targeting takes that forecast and compares it with a risk target you choose yourself. If your target is 10 % a year and the forecast for the market is 20 %, the market is twice as wild as you want, so you hold 10 / 20 = 50 % of your money in the market, and your risk stays at 10 %. In general: exposure = target volatility / forecast volatility. When the forecast is above your target, you hold less than all of your money. When it is below, the rule asks for more than 100 %, which means borrowing, so the exposure usually gets a cap.

One limit remains: every forecast looks back. A sudden crash after a calm stretch still hits a full position, and only afterwards does the forecast jump and the position shrink.

The code (vt_reel.py, 15 lines of Python with numpy) is general on purpose: a GARCH forecast for tomorrow from today's move and today's forecast (omega 0.05, alpha 0.10, beta 0.85 in percent squared per day, as in part 39), the rule exposure = target / forecast with a cap, and a daily loop over the returns that sets the exposure before each day and updates the forecast after it.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 42: Risk Parity. 

Bridgewater launched All Weather in 1996. Its scenarios are growth and inflation, each higher or lower than expected, and the goal is the same amount of risk in each of them. Bridgewater calls it the foundation of risk parity, which spreads the risk evenly across assets, usually whole asset classes like stocks, bonds and commodities.

Take a classic 60/40 portfolio. Stocks swing much more than bonds. Assuming 15 % volatility a year for stocks, 5 % for bonds and a correlation of 0.2, every dollar in stocks brings three times the risk, and stocks carry about 90 % of the portfolio's risk (91.8 %) while holding 60 % of the money. With a correlation anywhere from 0 to 0.3, the share stays between 90 % and 95 %.

Risk parity sets the weights so that each asset contributes the same share of the total risk. The simplest version is inverse volatility: w_i = (1/σ_i) / Σ_j (1/σ_j). With 15 % and 5 %, that gives 25 % stocks and 75 % bonds, and each causes exactly half of the portfolio's ups and downs. For two assets this holds for any correlation, because 0.25 × 15 = 0.75 × 5. With more assets, full risk parity solves for equal risk contributions w_i (Σw)_i / σ_p², the quantity the code calls risk_shares.

The catch is that this calmer mix usually earns less, so many risk parity funds borrow money to scale it up. And when stocks and bonds fall at the same time, the balance does not protect you.

The code (rp_reel.py, 14 lines of plain Python without packages) is general on purpose: the portfolio variance from weights and a covariance matrix, each asset's share of the risk, and inverse volatility weights that add up to 100 %.

caption:
➡️ Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 43: Black-Litterman. 

Fischer Black and Robert Litterman published it in 1992 as an improvement on the Markowitz optimizer. Markowitz needs each asset's expected return and volatility. Volatility is fairly easy to estimate, expected returns are very hard, and small errors in them push the weights to extremes.

Black-Litterman starts from the market portfolio instead: all the money invested in a market, with each asset's weight equal to its share of the total. As in the CAPM part, this portfolio is optimal in equilibrium, so the model works backwards and asks which returns would make it optimal. The answer is π = δΣw: the market weights w, the covariance matrix Σ (how strongly the assets swing and move together) and the risk aversion δ (extra return demanded per unit of risk) give the implied returns π.

Example with 60 % stocks and 40 % bonds, assuming 15 % volatility for stocks, 5 % for bonds, a correlation of 0.2 and δ = 2.5: stocks imply about 3.5 % above the risk free rate (3.525 %), bonds 0.475 %.

Then you add your own view, for example stocks earn 6 %, and say how sure you are. The model mixes market and view like a weighted average. If you are as sure as the market (view uncertainty Ω = τσ² with τ = 0.05), stocks land at about 4.8 % (4.7625 %), exactly halfway. Without any view you get back the market portfolio.

The code (bl_reel.py, 13 lines of plain Python without packages) is general on purpose: implied returns from risk aversion, covariance and weights, how much of your trust goes to your view, and the weighted average of market and view. For a single view on one asset this is exactly the full Black-Litterman formula.

➡️ Quantitative Finance from Scratch, part 44: Arbitrage Pricing Theory (APT). 

Stephen Ross published it in 1976 as an alternative to the CAPM. The CAPM explains expected returns with one risk, the market. The APT allows several risks, called factors, for example surprises in economic growth, inflation or interest rates. Every stock gets its own beta for each factor, plus swings of its own that have nothing to do with any factor.

A factor model describes how a return moves when a factor changes. The APT asks a different question: what return should an investor expect for carrying that risk? In a factor model each stock can have its own alpha. The APT says this alpha should be zero, because two stocks with the same exposures carry the same risk and should earn the same expected return.

The formula: E[R_i] = r_f + β_i1 λ_1 + β_i2 λ_2 + ... + β_iK λ_K, with r_f the risk free rate, β the exposure of the stock to one factor and λ the premium the market pays per unit of that factor's risk.

If two stocks have the same exposures and one is expected to earn more, you buy that one and sell the other. Every factor cancels out, and with many such pairs their own swings average away. Traders who exploit such gaps push prices back, so expected returns line up on the formula, at least approximately. The theory leaves open which factors to use; researchers pick them from data, like Chen, Roll and Ross (1986) with economic factors, and the Fama-French model follows the same logic.

The code (apt_reel.py, 15 lines of plain Python without packages) is general on purpose: the expected return from the risk free rate, the betas and the premiums, the alpha as the part the betas leave unexplained, and the arbitrage rule for two stocks with the same betas.

Sources: Ross, S. A. (1976), The Arbitrage Theory of Capital Asset Pricing, Journal of Economic Theory 13(3), 341-360. Chen, N.-F., Roll, R. and Ross, S. A. (1986), Economic Forces and the Stock Market, Journal of Business 59(3), 383-403.
